analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage in steps from $5.15 to $7.00 an hour.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise the minimum wage from $5.15 to $7.00 an hour was introduced in April 2004 with 27 cosponsors but never received a Senate vote before Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have lifted the federal minimum wage from $5.15 an hour in three steps: to $5.85 two months after passage, $6.45 a year later, and $7.00 two years later [S2] [S3]. It would also have extended the federal minimum wage to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands for the first time, phasing the island's lower wage up in 50-cent steps until it matched the national floor [S2] [S3]. The bill sat on the Senate calendar from May 2004 until the Congress ended and never came to a vote [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the minimum wage would see their hourly pay rise by up to $1.85 over two years, and workers in the Northern Mariana Islands would gain federal wage protections for the first time [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in three steps to $7.00 an hour, an increase of $1.85 over the then-current $5.15 rate
Extends federal minimum wage law to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, which had previously been exempt, phasing its wage up 50 cents every six months until it equals the federal floor

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay minimum-wage labor, most visibly restaurants, retail stores, and other low-wage service businesses, would bear higher payroll costs; in the Northern Mariana Islands, the garment industry and other employers would face a phased-in federal wage floor for the first time [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Low-wage service employers and CNMI businesses

drawbacks.text: The increase would raise labor costs for small businesses in restaurants, retail, and other low-margin industries that employ many minimum-wage workers, and some employers could respond by cutting hours or positions, as opponents of federal minimum wage increases routinely argue
The phased increase to $7.00 over two years would have partially eroded by inflation before the final step took effect, meaning the real raise was smaller than the nominal one

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers earning $5.15 an hour, a raise to $7.00 is a direct 36% pay increase, and the evidence on modest federal minimum wage increases shows limited employment loss relative to the wage gains. The main costs fall on low-wage employers, some of which are small businesses, and the two-year phase-in means the final increase would have lost some of its value to inflation. On balance, the gains to low-paid workers are large and the costs are diffuse and modest.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and placed on the Senate calendar in early May 2004, then sat there with no committee action and no floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Sen. Kennedy introduced the Fair Minimum Wage Act of 2004 on April 29, 2004, with 26 Senate cosponsors listed on the bill
The Senate read the bill twice and placed it on the legislative calendar under General Orders on May 3, 2004, Calendar No. 496
No further action was taken: the bill never received a committee hearing or a floor vote before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that pay minimum wage keep paying $5.15 an hour instead of a phased-in $7.00, and businesses in the Northern Mariana Islands, including its garment industry, remain outside the federal minimum wage system. Workers who would have received the raise are the direct losers.

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 29, 2004 and delivered introductory remarks

for.name: 26 Senate cosponsors
for.role: Democratic and independent senators who signed on, including Sens. Daschle, Boxer, Clinton, Kerry, and Edwards

against.name: Senate Republican leadership of the 108th Congress
against.role: Majority leadership controlling the Senate floor schedule
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote; it sat on the Senate calendar for eight months until the Congress ended

against.name: Jack Abramoff and the Northern Mariana Islands government lobbying effort
against.role: Lobbyists retained to keep federal wage law out of the CNMI
against.what_they_did: Lobbied Congress for years to block applying the federal minimum wage to the Northern Mariana Islands, the same provision this bill included

sides.party_line_note: All 28 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or one independent; no Republicans signed on, and the Republican-controlled Senate never scheduled a vote.

industries.note: The bill would raise their labor costs by up to $1.85 an hour per minimum-wage worker. Their interest in blocking the bill runs against the wage gains it would deliver to workers.

industries.industry: Northern Mariana Islands garment and other island employers
industries.note: The islands were exempt from the federal minimum wage, letting manufacturers pay workers far less than the national floor. The bill would have ended that exemption; its failure keeps the island economy outside federal wage law.
